title: Theo and the Horizon
premise: Rosalind Vane, captain of the riverboat Kestrel, is hired by her old rival Cassian Marsh to run contraband medicine upriver before the passes close — and discovers a stowaway, ten-year-old Theo, whose dead mother was the reason Rosalind and Cassian swore off smuggling years ago. The medicine is meant for the mountain settlement that failed Theo's mother, and delivering it means breaking the law to honor a promise the law never kept. Pursued by a customs cutter and betrayed by one of their own crew, they cross the range ahead of the snows; Rosalind delivers the medicine, gives Theo a place aboard as family, and lets go of the guilt she has been measuring in miles for three years.
about_author: Ines Okonkwo grew up between her grandmother's ferry landing on the Niger and a boarding school in Lagos, where she learned that rivers keep better records than courts. She now writes adventure novels from a houseboat, insisting that every plot must survive being read aloud over engine noise.

chapters.title: The Weight of Water
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Three years after a disaster she refuses to name, Rosalind pilots the Kestrel through fog-bound shallows, measuring her life in miles. A letter arrives bearing Cassian Marsh's seal — the rival she swore never to work with again. Emotional beat: restless grief disguised as routine, cracked open by the past knocking at the wheelhouse door.

chapters.title: An Old Debt in a New Harbor
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. In Port Merrow, Cassian offers triple pay for one run: sealed crates of medicine upriver to Highmoor Settlement before the snows close the pass. He won't say who paid him or why he needs her specifically. She refuses — until she sees the manifest's return address: the orphanage where her sworn-off life began. Beat: pride wrestling with an old wound.

chapters.title: The Boy Behind the Barrels
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, first time. A day out of port, deckhand Milo finds a stowaway: Theo, small, sharp-tongued, clutching his mother's brass compass. He claims Cassian owes her. Rosalind recognizes the compass instantly — it belonged to Wren, the woman whose death ended everything. Beat: fury curdling into reluctant protectiveness; the cargo suddenly has a face.

chapters.title: What Was Sworn Off
chapters.summary: Cassian's POV. Around the galley fire, Cassian confesses: Wren died waiting on medicine the law confiscated at the checkpoint, and these crates are the same shipment's replacement, funded quietly by the settlement itself. Justice outside the law, he argues, is still justice. Rosalind agrees to finish the run but not to forgive him. Beat: bitter reckoning, uneasy alliance forged.

chapters.title: The Cutter's Wake
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A customs cutter appears astern, tipped off by an informant aboard. Rosalind runs the Kestrel down the Sorrow Narrows — sandbars only she knows — while Theo, unafraid of heights, scrambles the mast to cut fouled rigging. They escape into reed marshes. Beat: exhilaration and trust; Theo stops being cargo and becomes crew.

chapters.title: The Traitor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Milo's POV. The informant is exposed: quartermaster Dree sold them out to save her brother from a customs prison. Rosalind must choose — maroon her or bind her to the mission. She chooses the latter, arguing that people break for love, not malice. Beat: moral complexity deepens; the crew becomes a fragile, chosen family.

chapters.title: Where the River Ends
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The river shallows to stones; the boat can go no farther. They abandon the Kestrel — Rosalind's true home — and take to mule track through the foothills as the first snows fall early. Theo falters, blaming himself for slowing them. Rosalind tells him about Wren honestly, for the first time. Beat: sacrifice, tenderness, shared memory replacing silence.

chapters.title: The Pass Called Mercy
chapters.summary: Cassian's POV. An avalanche seals the main pass; the only way through is Mercy Pass, a cliff route Cassian once survived and swore never to repeat. Dree's knowledge of customs patrol schedules buys them a night window. Halfway across, a rope fails and Cassian catches Theo, nearly falling himself. Beat: terror transmuted into redemption; the rival earns his second chance.

chapters.title: Highmoor
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Frostbitten and half-starved, they reach Highmoor as fever sweeps the settlement — the medicine arrives hours ahead of the worst. Theo watches his mother's compass given to the settlement's doctor, her promise finally kept through him. The customs officer who arrives behind them chooses, seeing the sick children, to log the crates as lost. Beat: catharsis; justice rendered outside the law, by choice.

chapters.title: Measuring in Years Again
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Spring. The rebuilt Kestrel waits at the river's mouth, and Theo stands at the rail with a crew badge stitched by Dree. Cassian asks, half-joking, whether there's room for a rival aboard. Rosalind says the horizon looks different when you're not running from it. Beat: belonging found, grief set down like ballast, the voyage truly beginning.
